newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania village residents in quandary over vote.
newsitem.headline: Albania village residents in quandary over vote.

text.p: Albanian villagers, their lives blighted by poverty and unemployment, are in a quandary over whether to back rightists for another four years or the Socialist alternative in Sunday's general election.

Most men lounging in the dusty streets of Vaqarr, 10 km (six miles) west of Tirana, or debating loudly in its sole bar, had yet to opt for President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party or the Socialists, heirs to Albania's hardline communists.
"Things have never been so difficult as now, not even under communism," said Pajtim Mehmeti, one of a dozen exclusively male customers downing grape-based raki liquor in the bar.
"There's no money for breeding livestock or irrigation. We've had to chop down the entire peach orchard. No one wants a return to communism, but no one's sure who to vote for either."
Villagers like Vaqarr's 1,400 residents make up more than 60 percent of Albania's 3.4 million population.

The Socialists, under economist Fatos Nano, have fought on a free market platform and say they will win. Both parties promise to end the violence which has killed 1,500 people since the collapse of pyramid investment schemes earlier this year.
The "pyramids" robbed countless thousands of Albanians of their savings, including residents of crumbling, rubbish-strewn Vaqarr. But the violence seems to have passed the village by.
Local chairmen of the Democratic and Socialist parties, far from lunging at each other's throats, drink at the same table.
Political ideology takes second place to traditional family -- and male-dominated -- values.
"Look, I've got 30 votes to offer," said Gani, invoking his right as head of household to tell family members how to vote. "Should I tell them to go for Sali (Berisha) or for the beard?"
That referred to Socialist Nano's neat, greying beard -- a facial feature banned during isolationist communist leader Enver Hoxha's four decades in power.
Gani wondered out loud about throwing the votes instead behind King Leka I, returned from nearly 60 years in exile in South Africa to campaign for restoration of the monarchy.

"It may appear quiet on the surface here but things are boiling just beneath it," said a man in his early 30s. Like most of those present, he had no job and relied on a small tract of land and a few cattle and goats to feed his family.
"This has affected all of us. My brother's a policeman and his daughter still puts her fingers in her ears at the mere sight of his pistol."
People waiting in Vaqarr's post office, where bare light bulbs hung from ceilings and paint was peeling off walls, had a more secure source of income -- they were phoning relatives working in Italy.
A clutch of men outside the communist-era "House of Culture", almost reduced to rubble and surrounded by weeds, debated what putting Nano in power would mean.
"Things were all right under Berisha until the pyramids went down," said Baftjar Driza.
"If Nano gets in, you'll be back working in a co-operative. How'd you like that?" retorted his friend Agim. Both laughed.
Vaqarr's womenfolk, used to performing most of the tasks inside and outside their homes, had less time to debate politics. They, too, were divided among the candidates.

"Seven years ago at least we had water in our homes," said Xheje Sula, 56, one of several women fetching water and washing clothes at a well. "Last time we voted for this president. Now I don't know. He didn't do what he said he would."
The lack of amenities no longer bothers Helena Holfman, an American missionary living in Vaqarr for four years. But she was far from certain the election would improve matters.
"I doubt elections will change much here," she said, trying to fix her home's separate water pump. "What Albanians need more than anything is education to understand democracy."
